opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the two are really two sides of the same coin. The very things that make these models so powerful and exciting are exactly the things that make responsible AI so much harder for them than it was for the previous generation of machine learning.

If you go back to the kind of work I and many others were doing on algorithmic fairness or privacy five or ten years ago, we were mostly thinking about fairly narrow predictive models. You have a model that decides who gets a loan, or predicts recidivism, or screens resumes. In that setting the task is well defined, the output is a number or a yes-or-no decision, and you can write down fairly crisp mathematical definitions. You can say, for instance, that the false positive rates should be roughly equal across racial groups, and then you can measure it, audit for it, and even build it into the training algorithm as a constraint.

Generative AI breaks a lot of that. First, the outputs are open-ended. They're paragraphs of text, images, code, and it's much harder to say precisely what it means for a paragraph of text to be "fair" or "unbiased." Second, these models are general purpose. The same model might be drafting a legal memo in one minute and writing a children's story the next, and the norms for what counts as appropriate or harmful vary across those use cases. So the specification problem, deciding what we even want, has gotten a lot harder.

There are also some genuinely new concerns. Hallucination, or what I'd rather call confabulation, wasn't really a thing with a loan model. Intellectual property and the provenance of training data become serious issues when the model can reproduce things very close to what it was trained on. Privacy takes on a different character, because the model might regurgitate pieces of its training data verbatim. And there's toxicity and the potential for misuse, which grow precisely because the models are so capable and so easy to use.

That said, I'm not purely pessimistic. Some of the scientific approaches we developed still carry over: differential privacy, for example, gives you meaningful guarantees about memorization if you're willing to pay the cost in accuracy and compute. And the power of these models can be turned toward the problem itself. You can use generative models to help red-team other models, to generate test cases at scale, or to assist in auditing. So I'd say the power creates the challenges, but it may also be part of the toolkit for addressing them. We're just at a much earlier stage scientifically than we were with the narrower models, and I think the field needs to be humble about how much we actually know how to guarantee right now.

r001.rationale: The response links the models’ power to responsible-AI difficulty, then identifies open-ended outputs as a challenge. It does not clearly say that open-endedness is itself a source of their power.

r002.rationale: It says open-ended outputs make it harder to define fairness and bias, directly identifying open-endedness as a source of responsible-AI challenges.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the short version is that the things that make generative models so powerful are exactly the things that make responsible AI harder, not easier.

If you go back to the era I spent a lot of time in, the classical machine learning setting, the models were narrow. You trained a model to do one thing: predict whether somebody would repay a loan, classify an image, flag a transaction as fraudulent. And because the task was narrow, the responsibility questions were narrow too. You could write down what fairness meant for that task. You could say, here's the protected group, here's the error rate I care about, here's the constraint I want to enforce. You could reason about privacy because you knew what the training data was and what the output was. The science of responsible AI, as it developed over the last decade or so, was largely built around that one-model, one-task picture.

Generative models blow that up. A large language model isn't trained to do a task; it's trained to do, in some sense, everything. It's an open-ended artifact. The user supplies the task at inference time, in natural language, and the space of possible tasks is essentially unbounded. So when someone asks me, "Is this model fair?", my honest reaction is, fair at what? Fair when it's summarizing resumes? Fair when it's writing a cover letter? Fair when it's giving medical information to a user who hasn't told it their demographic? Each of those is a different question, and the model is the same model.

And the same thing happens with the other pillars. Privacy: these models are trained on enormous scrapes of the internet, and we know they can memorize and regurgitate content, but defining what a privacy violation even is when the data wasn't collected in a structured way is genuinely hard. Explainability: the old interpretability tools were already shaky on deep networks, and now we have hundreds of billions of parameters and emergent behaviors nobody designed. Robustness: the model will happily behave in ways nobody anticipated because nobody could enumerate the inputs.

So I'd put it this way. The power comes from generality, and generality is the enemy of the kind of precise specification that responsible AI depends on. We spent years learning how to bake constraints into the training process. With generative models, a lot of the mitigation has moved to after the fact: red teaming, guardrails, filtering, fine-tuning with human feedback. Those are useful, but they're fundamentally reactive and empirical. You're playing whack-a-mole with an object whose behavior you can't fully characterize.

That said, I don't think it's hopeless. I think it means the research agenda has to shift. Instead of asking "is this model fair" in the abstract, we need to ask it in the context of specific deployments, with specific users and specific stakes, and develop auditing methods that scale to open-ended behavior. And I think there's a real opportunity for the algorithmic approaches, the differential privacy and fairness-constrained learning ideas, to find their way into these systems, but it's going to take some real work to adapt them. We're at the beginning of that, not the end.

r001.rationale: The response says generative models’ power comes from their generality and describes them as open-ended, able to handle essentially unbounded tasks.

r002.rationale: The response connects that generality to responsible AI challenges, saying it makes precise specification harder and complicates fairness, privacy, explainability, and robustness.

astra-6.text:
I think the power and the challenges are very closely connected. The more general-purpose a model is, the more useful things it can do, but the harder it becomes to characterize all the ways it might fail. With a model built for a narrow prediction task, you can at least specify the setting in which you want to measure accuracy, fairness, or privacy. With a generative model, people can use it in ways that its developers never anticipated.

That makes responsible AI partly a question of what you can guarantee about the underlying model, and partly a question of how you deploy it. Who is using it? What decisions depend on its output? What happens when it makes a mistake? The same error can be inconsequential in one application and quite damaging in another.

And greater capability doesn’t automatically resolve those issues. A model can become more fluent and useful without becoming more reliable in every setting. So we need to advance our ability to evaluate and constrain these systems alongside our ability to make them more powerful.

r001.rationale: It connects a model’s general-purpose breadth—its ability to do more things—to its usefulness, conveying open-endedness as a source of power.

r002.rationale: It says generative models can be used in unanticipated ways and that their failures are harder to characterize, conveying open-endedness as a responsible AI challenge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think their power and the challenges are closely connected. What makes these models so compelling is that they can be applied to an enormous range of tasks. But that same generality makes it difficult to characterize where they’ll work well, where they’ll fail, and what the consequences of those failures might be.

With a more narrowly defined machine learning system, you can at least start with a particular application and ask concrete questions about fairness, privacy, or accuracy. With a generative model, those questions depend heavily on how somebody uses it. The same model might help someone write a poem or provide advice that they treat as authoritative in a consequential decision. Those require very different standards.

So I don’t think we should expect a single declaration that a model is responsible or safe. We need to examine specific properties, in specific settings, and be explicit about what we can measure and what remains uncertain. As the capabilities expand, the work of doing that becomes more important—and harder.

r001.rationale: It says the models are compelling because they apply to an enormous range of tasks, identifying their generality as a source of power.

r002.rationale: It says that same generality makes it hard to predict performance, failures, and consequences, linking open-endedness to responsible AI challenges.
